The House having under consideration the bill to establish Soldiers Home, Mr. LIEFEVRE said:

Mr. SPEAKER being novice in matters of legislation, and young in experience, when I took my seat in this Hall, I resolved rather to be a learner than an instructor. But, sir, I feel that I would not discharge the duty I owe to myself and the disabled soldiers of Ohio, were I to remain silent upon a subject upon which hinges their happiness and comfort.

In the first place, I wish to say that I am not in favor of establishing a permanent home for disabled soldiers at this time, and the bill which we have under consideration does not propose to do any such thing, as has been inferred by gentlemen upon this floor. It merely provides to furnish a home for those disabled soldiers who have no paternal shelter; who cannot look in the prospective to loving arms and warm hearts to encircle and shelter them; but who are dependent upon those charities of the world which we all know to be cold and careless. It only provides for them the coming year, and if Congress fails to make the proper provision, when we return here next winter, we can make such permanent arrangement as the exigencies of the case may seem to warrant. It is plain, in my mind, that the object of the honorable gentleman from Scioto (Mr. Clover) is to defeat the bill, and force the House to adhere to the incomplete and inefficient substitute he has proposed. His institute would send these unfortunate braves back to their counties, townships and Congressional districts with an empty promise to their ear, which would be blighted in the realization, that they will be cared for by those communities. Has there been any means for their support elsewhere? No, sir; it is only an empty promise, having no warrant of law to fulfill it. What will be the result of his proposed action? The question is easily answered. Those who are not able to earn livelihood, will soon fill our county infirmaries or our jails. Every gentleman on this floor who participated in recruiting regiment or company, knows what these promises amount to. How many poor men, with families, put their names on the enlistment roll, strapped on their knapsacks, and marched to the field of conflict upon the promise that while they were gone, their wives and children should be cared for? Those of us who were in the field know too well how those promises were kept. They were broken in almost every instance. No sooner was the soldier in the field than they were forgotten, and how often has the heart sickened and the ear been pained to listen to the story of their privations and suffering. Those men did not go out to fight for counties or districts, but for the great State of Ohio, and it is the duty of the generous old State to do justice to her defenders. The Honorable gentleman from Scioto objects to the bill because it discriminates, and only provides for the care of a portion of them. The Relief law is still in force and the Relief fund obtainable, and those who wish to remain with their families have the benefit of this reservoir for succor. The gentleman, referring to the present inmates of the Home, says that they were not the bone and sinew of the army but that they are Dutch and Irish mendicants and beggars. I answer the gentleman upon that point, with the remark that they had sufficient bone and sinew to march into the jaws of death for the preservation of their country, and were rescued with broken down constitutions, maimed and crippled for life, and that many of them have toiled through the dreary marshes, and on the desolate plains and wearisome mountains, with Grant, with Thomas, with Sheridan, with Custer and with Sherman, down to the sea, and are entitled not to contemplate epithets, but to the gratitude of a nation. It may be that they are Dutch or Irish; but it is enough to us to know that they are afflicted soldiers, and that they enlisted under the banner of the stars to preserve its purity and unity.

Who are the gentlemen opposing this bill? Are they men who have served in the field and borne the heat and burden of the day? No, sir; and I rejoice that no soldier upon this floor has objected to the bill. Its opponents are the extremely coy men who have fought valiantly in the rear, under the leadership of Dorsey G. Jones, who have grown rich off of the grandeur of the nation, and are fearful that the passage of the bill will cost them few of their precious ducats.

Our noble old Buckeye State has achieved the chief prominence in the war, not only by the large armies she sent into the field and the brilliant genius she gave, but by her devotion to the comfort and welfare of her soldiers; and now, at the close of the great struggle, she can cap the climax of her renown by giving to her disabled privates—the heroes of the war—a resting place and home, where they can live under the beneficent hand of a magnanimous patron and guardian.

The State of West Virginia is about to build its first Penitentiary. The writer of this article understands that it has not yet been finally determined what system of discipline shall be adopted in administration, and feeling a deep interest in the decision which may be reached, he begs leave to SUBMIT some considerations upon the subject involved. It may be proper for him to add that by this discussion he proposes to aid the public authorities in the selection of that plan which will best accomplish the ends for which a State prison is constructed.

Two systems of discipline are now in use in the various civilized countries of the world. One has come to be known with us as the "silent" or Auburn system. The peculiarity of this plan is that it allows the prisoners to associate together during the day in their workshops, but in order to prevent the evils which are acknowledged to flow from unrestricted intercourse among themselves, it imposes the most rigid silence upon them, and requires them at night to be confined each one by himself. The convicts are not permitted to speak to each other; though they may address necessary inquiries to their instructors or keepers; and they may converse with the chaplain, and join to a certain extent in the religious exercises provided in the institution.

The other plan is known as the "separate" or Pennsylvania SYSTEM. The peculiarity of it is, that it requires the prisoners to be kept entirely separate from each other, so that even the personal appearance, if possible, of any one may be unknown to any other of the convicts. At the same time it furnishes them with suitable and sufficient employment in their cells, provides books for general reading and for study, and affords both intellectual and religious instruction either in the cells or in some room where the convicts may be assembled without seeing each other. This plan permits the officers of the prison and to visit the convict, and allows his friends, under supervision, to correspond with him. In some instances a little garden is given to him to cultivate for himself; and such appliances may be introduced into his cell as to render it more comfortable than the ordinary sleeping rooms of many of his fellow men outside of the walls. The distinguishing popularity of the system, it will be observed, is that the prisoners are kept entirely separate from each other. The idea of what is popularly called solitary confinement may be as much intercourse with the officers of the institution or with other people as the most tender-hearted philanthropist could desire.

Which of these two plans is, on the whole, preferable? Which of them would it be advisable for the State of West Virginia to adopt for the institution located at Moundsville? The writer presumes that most persons would, like himself, at first thought, by their prejudices and imperfect acquaintance with the subject, be led to feel and express a very decided preference for the silent or Auburn plan. But at the same time he believes, that just as he by investigation has been convinced of the clear superiority of the separate, or Pennsylvania system, so also others by like process may be brought to a like conclusion.

The object of imprisonment in a penitentiary is twofold. Its legitimate use is to punish criminals with view to the protection of society, and also, if possible, to achieve the moral reformation of the criminal. There are also, it will be noticed, two parties concerned namely, society and the criminal—and these two parties have certain rights which should be preserved in any plan of discipline which may be adopted. As long ago as 1787, Bentham, the well known philanthropist laid down these rights in substantially the following form. His statement is still sufficiently accurate for our present purpose. He conceived the prisoner to be entitled to "the air, wholesome and sufficient food, protection from cold, opportunities of exercise, the privilege of labor, and the devotion of part of the proceeds of that labor to the support of his family, if he has one."

He also argued that society has right to demand "that the prisoner shall be securely confined, and that he shall not be made worse either in body or character by his imprisonment; that his intemperance or other evil habits shall be restrained, and that education and religious instruction shall be provided for him." The question for us now to settle is, what system best meets these conditions, and accomplishes the great twofold design of a state prison.

Now we may freely admit that convicts even where separated from each other in different cells will in some cases succeed in holding intercourse. Absolute isolation is a dream which is not likely to be realized, so long as more than one convict is confined in the same building. Fare thee well, my good old knapsack!
I must part with thee at last;
Since I took thee as companion
We have weathered many a blast;
Through the siege in front of Yorktown
And in the fields at Williamsburgh,
Thou hast braved it out, old fellow,
Staunch in battle thou hast stood.
Whom dark night had closed the carnage,
Of that sad though deathless day,
When we bivouacked so weary,
By cold Chickahominy;
When dead and dying all around us
Strewed the ground at Seven Pines,
Then found the worth old knapsack,
Of such virtues as were thine.
Mechanicsville and Gaines' Mill,
Each have tried thy sinews well;
Savage Station and Peach Orchard
All thy many virtues tell.
At Malvern Hill thou viewed the slaughter,
Of the rebs by our bayonets driven;
And when by James our feet we planted,
A brief, sad respite thee was given.
And Gettysburg and stern Antietam,
Alike bear thee witness;
Spottsylvania and Cold Harbor
Ever found thee in the skirmish;
Petersburgh again beheld thee
As met its overthrow;
And thy march with me was onward
Till unslung in Richmond,
When heartsick, sad and footsore,
In the trench all night lay,
Thinking of to-morrow's battle,
And of dear ones far away;
Behind the breast-works waiting the onset
Darksome looked the world to me;
But all save the old knapsack,
Could fail of loving thee?
Thou wert ever true, old comrade,
Thou to me wert ever true;
I have carried thee in summer,
And when piercing Northers blew;
When my friends had all deserted,
When my foes looked doubly black,

Still found thee at my back.

Midst the mud and swamp,
While conned mother's letter,
Moon or watch-fire's lamp,

Breathing in me childhood's spell,
Calling home the hayward wanderer,
But now to tell.
But, worn out in service,
Neath the sod shall be laid down,
When no more the grim war's battle
Shall confront me with its frown,
May some noble-hearted comrade
Find thee to my memory,
As honest tears, old knapsack,
As are falling now for thee.

OCCASIONAL.

The following article, from the pen of Ex-Governor Allen, of Louisiana, and now editor of the American Times, is clipped from that paper of the 9th of January. It is composition worthy of the immortal Junius. In its power, in its force of bitterness and sentiment, it is an unequaled piece of writing. Of the personality of the article we have nothing to say, but submit it to our readers as a specimen of most extraordinary composition.

The civil war in America is ended, and the banner of the bars that waved over Jackson, and cleaned upon the track of Stuart's reckless riders has been put away as men hide the trinkets of dear, dead love.

Although the blood of Virginia's best and bravest is not yet dry in the valleys, nor has the grass grown over the premature graves of the manly Confederates who fell before Petersburg, yet Mr. E. W. Pollard, pretty writer and talented editor, in a long newspaper article, denounces ex-President Davis, Generals Lee, Johnston and Beauregard, and says "the Southern people disgraced themselves forever when they refused to fight to determination; that they lack courage and endurance—statesmanship acknowledgement: criticises campaigns, ridicules strategic movements, sneers at retreats, and laughs at every heroic effort of the brave men who have left to history an immortal name."

Who is Mr. E. W. Pollard? He is Virginian, the editor of the Richmond Examiner, and the author of "The Southern History of the War." We have grief for the first, blushes for the second, and contempt for the last.

During all those years of carnage and of blood, this Richmond Examiner was an insatiate friend of opposition and hatred. Step by step it broke down the brave, fond heart of Sidney Johnston again and again; it lacerated and gouged the sensitive soul of Beauregard; week after week it denounced the heroic efforts of Joseph E. Johnston; and now, when Jefferson Davis is chained amid the waves of his rock-ribbed prison, it tries to stab his reputation and his honor.

It is not often that men like Pollard and Jordan can gloat over the agony of such spirit and the degradation of such a name. It is not often that such honor is laid bare for the thrust of every ruffian's spear, or the dagger of every towards hand. It is not often that a desolated nation writhes under the blows of its children and the cruelties of its own offspring. It is not often that the world furnishes human hyenas to exhume the bodies of her sainted dead, and howl in horrid delight over the revolving feast.

Pollard wanted determination, but he was in New York city, hob-nobbing with freebooters, and telling the pleasant story in his pleasant way of the four years war. He wanted fifty thousand men to fight a million to the death, but he never fell in beside them and proffered to share common fate. Like Jobs war-horse, he snuffed the battle from afar! Shoddy is cheap, and humbug is cheap, and Henry Ward Beecher's patent sermons are cheap; and sincerity, faith, honor, chivalry, manhood! how pure and unpopular.

Pollard's mother State lies prostrate in the dust, her hearth-stones desolate and her idol shattered. All over the land he can see her bereaved daughters weeping for the young, fresh faces that looked back to them from the heat and yellow dust of the conflict just before the horses trod them down. He can almost hear the breezes from the Wilderness singing their melancholy dirges over Stuart and Ashby, and Pickens, and Hill, and Jackson. Dear to God, he has no love, nor veneration, nor tenderness, nor pity for any of these; but tearing open the graves of the immortalized dead, he blends them with the living in one sacrilegious anathematizing hatred.

Drape the picture of a nation in its agony, and cover its laurels with the mourning cypress; furl the conquered banner with farewell look, and shrine its memory in our heart of hearts; but to the brutal hardihood of those who curse and villify a ruined race, give vengeance, scorn, and an ever-dying contempt.

History tells how Coriolanus halted his victorious legions beyond the Yellow Tiber, but that Nero filled a goodly time while Rome was burning. Amid the graves of his kinsmen, the anguish and despair of brave men in their crushing overthrow, amid the blue skies and green fields of his nativity, a Pollard dips his pen in the gall of the New England hate and writes the record of his own everlasting infamy and disgrace.

DR. BOURNE, Dear Sir, It is with

Bourne, who stated that trip to the Islands

at his establishment. I placed myself under
his treatment, and in one week was so much
improved that I could risk returning home
and do my duty as Engineer on the Central
Pacific Railroad. The Doctor objected, but

WHY SHOULD WE WISH THE NEGROES TO

Emigrate?


Congress, as is well known, has appropriated
millions of acres of land in Florida, as well as in
Arkansas and other Western States, for the
benefit of the lately emancipated negroes of the
South. These negroes can, if they wish, emigrate
to these lands and, upon certain easy con-
ditions, become possessors of valuable farms. It
is thought that large emigration of blacks will
take place from South Carolina in the course of
the present fall and coming winter. We cannot
think that this is particularly desirable. White
laborers have not come among us yet; and, as
far as we can see, are not likely to come soon,
that is, in any considerable numbers. At all
events, South Carolina had better not lose one
class of laborers before she is certain of gaining
another.


We have lost the wealth which was invested in
slave property. And this is the greatest pecuni-
ary loss that any war has ever inflicted, or that
any people has ever suffered. If the Courts of
the country shall ultimately decide that the
emancipated slaves shall be paid for, we shall be
rejoiced; but we have little hope of it. We be-
lieve that right and justice, law and equity, de-
mand that they should be paid for. But all
questions of this class, in this country and at
this time, are beclouded by uncertainty.


We have this consolation however that what
individuals have lost in property, the country has
gained in population, properly considered. The
negroes were not properly population before; they
are now. And, in proportion as they become
settled reliable, and productive as free laborers
many advantages will accrue to the country to
counterbalance, in some degree, the disadvant-
ages it has suffered. In proportion as they become
successful laborers and producers, it will have
the effect upon the country as the free labor
and production of just so many white people. It
is true we cannot yet determine as to what stand-
ard of robustness and success they will reach as
laborers and producers; but we have great hope
that, upon the whole, free black labor will prove
reasonable success. At all events, let us give
the blacks every chance and every encouragement.
We are not inclined to think that they will prove
themselves totally unworthy of liberal opportun-
ity and enlightened encouragement. We have
been forced to yield our ownership of negroes.
They are now to us no longer, in any sense,
chattels. Let us take another step, rendered
necessary by their freedom, and regard them in a
higher sense than we did of yore; as human be-
ings subject to the same impulses in some degree,
governed by the same influences, and, on the
whole, very much like any other human being,
in the same position in society. It behooves us
now to give the negro perfectly fair chance, and
let him prove what he is capable of.


And reasoning upon the basis of successful
free black labor, how much greater will be the
material prosperity, say, of our rich plant-
ing regions, than it has ever been before! Take
a vicinity where there is not more than thirty or
forty white families, and perhaps a thousand
black families. Under the old system these
white families constituted the only patronage to
any merchants, mechanics, schools or churches,
in that vicinity. And that patronage was worth
little or nothing. The planters spent their money
where they pleased, and generally where it did
nothing toward the development of their region
of country, except in the way of enlarging its
few plantations.


Now, however, the money which will be made
in such region will be distributed among
population of thousand families, instead of
thirty or forty; and the most of it will be spent
where it is made. The effect can at once be seen.
Stores, dry goods and grocery establishments,
blacksmith and carpenter shops, homemakers,
churches and schools, and all the employments
and vocations necessary to so large population,
will at once spring up. The money which was
once taken out of the country, and never brought
back, being spent in distant cities and watering
places, will be retained in the country; and will
foster the different departments into which its
industry is divided.


And not only do the blacks become population
in the true sense; but their becoming population,
and the retention of their money in the country,
will be the means of adding largely to the white
population. Many kinds of business will bring
white people hither from abroad. Not only will
business flourish, and the waste lands, held by
large property owners, to the great injury of the
country, be settled and cultivated, but lands and
property of every kind, will rise in value. Pro-
duce of every kind will find market at home;
and the production of all those minor necessaries,
which our country is so well calculated to pro-
duce, and which, under the old system, were so
neglected, will be wonderfully stimulated.


These effects are already being witnessed in
many parts of the South. Let us accept the
situation and make the most of it. We may
regret the loss of the old civilization. Let us
console and compensate ourselves, as much as
we may do, by availing ourselves of the material
prosperity which the new situation offers.

FROM the Chicago Times.
The present is a crisis in the democratic
party which has no precedent in its history
as it is a crisis in the progress of the country
which is also without precedent. Never before
has the democratic party encountered
events so seriously affecting its future vitality
as now. Not that it beholds itself diminished
in the magnitude of its numbers,—for it is
numerically stronger than it has ever been
before—but it, having been beaten on a
great national issue, as to which it believed
itself to be wholly right and the opposition
wholly wrong, and still so believes, it must
nevertheless abandon that issue—for the de-
cision of it is final—and either sit down in
helpless and decaying inactivity, or strike
boldly out upon a new line, selected with par-
ticular reference, not to things as it would
have them, but to things as they actually are,
and in pursuing which line it shall cease to
be a mere Shack or CONSERVATIVE party, and
become, what it was in its prime days, pro-
gressive and an aggressive party. These are
the alternatives.
It will not sit down in helpless and decay-
ing inactivity.
What then shall the new line be? In the
first place, must we not cut loose from the
administration of Andrew Johnson, and
leave that hybrid concern to float on the sea
of public contempt into which it some time
since entered, and from which no power can
rescue it? Is not the late defeat at all largely
due to this administration than to
all other causes combined? What is there
in its composition to command public con-
fidence? Who, belonging to it, is entitled,
by reason of his antecedents or by his states-
manship, to the confidence of the respec-
tive democratic party! Certainly not
Andrew Johnson, nor William H. Seward,
nor Edwin M. Stanton. True, this adminis-
tration had right policy, and the democrats
party, in overlooking these men com-
prising it, and thinking only of the right-
ness of the policy, displayed prudence
whose policy was never exceeded; but the
policy having failed and having failed, too,
through the weakness and folly and offence,
against public propriety, of this administration,
why should not the democratic party
abandon the dead body, to whose adherence
which is death also?
What next? Can the democratic party
succeed until the negro question shall be got-
ten out of the way? It cannot. What next?
Is not negro suffrage inevitable, and is not
the quickest way to get the negro question
out of the way, to at once concede the suf-
frage which it shall be coerced to accept? We know
that many democrats have not reached this
advanced view of the case, and that such still
feel greatly inclined to revolt at the proposi-
tion of negro suffrage in any degree; but let
us tell them that it is ALWAYS wise to accept
the inevitable when the inevitable comes.
Negro suffrage, we say, is inevitable, and
whether it shall be qualified or universal
depends upon the promptness or otherwise
with which the democratic party shall move
with reference to it. The South will speedily
yield qualified negro suffrage upon the mo-
tion of the democratic party because it for
no other reason, she will soon see, if she does
not already see, that if she does not yield it,
she will ultimately be compelled to accept
universal negro suffrage.
Qualified negro suffrage wielded by the
SOUTH and by this we mean IMPARTIAL SUF-
FRAGE, or suffrage dependent upon the intel-
ligence of the man, irrespective of color, as
is now in Massachusetts, THE NEGRO
QUESTION WILL HAVE BEEN DISPOSED OF, AND
THE OCCUPATION OF THE NORTH REBUILT.
THE RADICAL PARTY WILL BE GONE FOREVER.
Not one inch of ground will it have to stand
upon and the country can once more turn
to those material questions of public policy
the right disposition of which is so essential
to the public prosperity. It will be upon
these questions that the democratic party
will triumph, and it will be by this triumph
that constitutional government and our fed-
eral system will be preserved.
If the South be wise, it will not wait, on
this suffrage question, even for the motion of
the democratic party. If it be wise, it will
lose no time in putting in motion the neces-
sary machinery by which it will at the same
time save itself from humiliation, preserve
its own self-respect, rid the country of the
most vexatious question that ever distracted
any country, kill the worst political party that
ever existed on the globe, and put the
way of speedy restoration.
This machinery consists, of course, in con-
ventions to revise the state constitutions.

Andrew Johnson on Vetoes.

In 1859, both Houses of Congress passed the homestead bill by more than a
two third vote. President Buchanan
vetoed the bill, and when it was returned, Andrew Johnson, then a Senator,
discussed the conduct of the President
in the following choice terms:

AN EXECUTIVE VETO A SMALL AFFAIR.
Notwithstanding the veto message
upon this homestead bill is long one,
and presents many arguments and state
ments as reasons for the veto, I am free
to say that the message has not wrought
the slightest change in my mind. The
fact of these reasons being sent here by
the President of the United States, it is
true, entitles them to consideration;
but their solidity and soundness are to
be examined just the same as if they
had been presented by anybody else;
and the mere fact of President of the
United States vetoing a bill makes no
change in my mind as to its propriety
and constitutionality, unless he presents
reasons and arguments which, if pre-
sented by others, would have the same
effect.

A PERSONAL SLAP AT OLD BUCK.

The argument upon the unconstitu-
tionality by the President is simply ab-
surd, not to say ridiculous, after the
long established usage of the Govern-
ment, receiving the sanction of nearly
every President of the United States.---
Gen. Jackson earnestly looked
forward to the day when the public
lands would cease to be a source of pub-
lic revenue, and pass into the hands of
the honest cultivator. It was his anx-
ious desire for the time to come when
every head of family in the United
States would be domiciliated, and have
children. Whether considerations so
rational, so humane, so Christian have
ever penetrated the brain of one whose
bosom has never yet swelled with
emotions for wife or children, is for all
enlightened public to determine.

HOW SENATORS SHOULD TREAT VETO.
I always have respect for a man who
fills the place of the President of the
United States, irrespective of party, and
it would be very natural for me to have
the utmost respect for his position, but
I cannot show my respect for a man of
character of great principles and truths
if he is not a man of character.
Does it make wrong right, or right
wrong? If there is great fundamen-
tal principle in this measure, connected
with Government and the great cause
of humanity, the fact that he withholds
his approval does not change my opin-
ion. I would stand by this and give
my vote and sanction to it, and I am
constrained to say that I look
upon this objection to the bill as mere
quibble on the part of the President,
and as such has been pressed for some en-
sure: and his allusion to principles
in this connection looks to me more
like the calculation of the mere poli-
tician and the demagogue than a grave
and sound reason to be offered by the
President of the United States in his veto
message upon so important a measure
as the homestead bill.

I have often heard that this world is
all making show; that it is constantly
changing; men are changing. These
are changing and revolutionary times.
O, consistency! thou art a jewel! much to be admired but
very much wanted in life now. I am not
inclined to attack his inconsistencies, but the fact that he
is inconsistent, and changes his opinion
with reference to great measure and a
great principle, is no reason why a Sen-
ator or Representative, who has acted
understandingly upon his own deliber-
ate judgment on a measure that has
been discussed for fifteen years in Con-
gress and before the people, should
change his opinion.

He has no right to dictate to the American people
and to the two Houses of Congress, in vio-
lation of the spirit, if not the letter, of the
constitution, that this measure
should not become law. Why do I say
this? Is there any difference in
the spirit of the constitution whether
a measure is sanctioned by a two thirds
vote before its passage or afterward?
When a measure has been vetoed by
the President, the constitution requires
that it shall be reconsidered and passed
by a two thirds vote, in order to become
a law.

The paper will be known under the above title, and have named it, only to localize and popularize it, but in honor of him who lived with and who died for us, and whose memory will be revered so long the everlasting mountains shall endure, which encompass his last resting place. and I am afraid you have come too late. How-
ever, I will make the proposition now. We
have in Fort Sumter with Major Anderson
about eighty men, and I learn from Major An-
derson that his provisions are nearly exhausted.
I have not only written to Governor Pickens,
but have sent special messenger to him, to
say that if he will allow Major Anderson to ob-
tain his marketing at the Charleston market, or
will have it sent to him, I will make no effort
to provision the fort; but if he does not do that,
I will not permit these people to starve, and
shall send a vessel loaded with bread and that
if he fires on that vessel he will fire upon an
unarmed vessel; but I shall at the same time
send fleet along with her, with instructions
not to enter the harbor of Charleston unless that
vessel is fired into, and if she is, then the fleet
is to enter the harbor and protect her. Now,
Mr. Baldwin, that fleet is now lying in the har-
bor of New York, and will be ready to sail this
afternoon at five o'clock. Although I fear it is
almost too late, yet I will submit the PROPOSE-
tion which I intended when I sent for Mr. Sum-
mers. Your convention in Richmond has been
sitting nearly two months, and all that they
have done has been to shake the rod over my
head. You have recently taken a vote in the
Virginia Convention on the right of secession,
which was rejected by 80 to 45, majority of
two-thirds, showing the strength of the Union
party in that convention. If you will go back
to Richmond and get that Union majority to
adjourn and go home without passing the ordi-
nance of secession, so anxious am I for the
preservation of the peace of this country, and
to save Virginia and the other Border States
from going out, that I will take the responsi-
bility of evacuating Fort Sumter, and take the
chance of negotiating with the Cotton States,
which have already gone out." "Well, Mr.
Lincoln," inquired Mr. Bolts, "how did Mr.
Baldwin respond?" Mr. Lincoln raising up his hands, "he
would not listen to it for a moment; he hardly
treated me with civility. He asked me what I
meant by an adjournment. Did I mean an ad-
journment sine die? Why, of course, Mr.
Baldwin, said I, I mean an adjournment sine
die. I do not mean to assume such a respon-
sibility as that of surrendering that fort to the
people of Charleston upon your adjournment,
and then for you to return in a week or ten days
and pass your ordinance of secession after I
have given up the fort."


Mr. Bolts, very much incensed, as he says,
that Mr. Baldwin should have rejected the
proposition, asked Mr. Lincoln to authorize him
to make it to the Union men of the Convention,
assuring him that they would adopt it willingly
and cheerfully, to which Mr. Lincoln replied,
"Oh, it is too late; the fleet has sailed, and
I have no means of communicating with it."
Mr. Bolts then asked permission to mention
the circumstances for Mr. Lincoln's own bene-
fit, but Mr. Lincoln said, "Well, not just now,
Bolts, after a while you may." Mr. Bolts'
inference was that Mr. Lincoln was assuming a
responsibility which would at that day have
been extremely distasteful to those who had
elevated him to the Presidency, but he thought
it due now to history, and to the character of
Mr. Lincoln, to make it known.


Mr. Bolts was here asked the question, "Are
you perfectly sure, according to your best recol-
lection, that Mr. Lincoln told you that he had
made that proposition to Mr. Baldwin, to evac-
uate Fort Sumter on this condition?" Answer,
"I know it as well as I know you are standing
before me and that I am answering your ques-
tion."


Mr. Bolts relates that some weeks afterwards
he returned to Richmond and mentioned one
evening to Mr. Jno. T. Lewis, a Union member
of the Convention, the substance of the con-
versation he had with Mr. Lincoln, and that next
morning Mr. Lewis and Mr. Baldwin drove to
his house, and had an interview with him,
which he narrates as follows:


"Well, Mr. Baldwin," said Mr. Bolts, "is it
true that Mr. Lincoln did propose to you that
if the Convention would adjourn and go home
without passing the ordinance of secession he
would evacuate Fort Sumter?"


"Yes," said Mr. Baldwin, "he did."


"My God, Mr. Baldwin," said Bolts, "why
did you reject such a proposition as that?"


The only answer that Baldwin made was by
taking out his watch and saying, "It only wants
twenty minutes of the hour of the meeting of
the Convention, when a most important vote is
to be taken," meaning the vote on the ordinance
of secession. "I am obliged to be there punct-
ually at the hour, and have not time to make
the explanation I desire, but will avail myself
of the earliest opportunity to make full ex-
planation."

If Congress had proposed to the States an amendment of the Constitution to the effect that in all elections for President or members of Congress, all male citizens in every State, whether white or black, should be entitled to vote, there would have been, notwithstanding the vast disparity of the black race in the several States, some little semblance of fairness in the proposition; because if adopted, each State would alike be compelled to allow the black race the right of suffrage; but the proposed alternative, whilst it compels every State where slavery lately existed to suffer the negro to vote, or incur the penalty of material reduction in its representatives, allows, in effect, to all the other States in view of the striking proportion that the black race in each of them bears to the white, the option of suffering the negro to vote or not as they may think proper, without the least possible danger of abridging the number of their representatives, if they prefer to exclude him. SPANISH GOVERNMENT.
From an official Correspondent.

The Spanish papers have recently made great NOISE
about the decree of the Queen suspending the duties on ex-

measure, which is highly celebrated to the Spanish Govern-

to the condition of other peoples and other

governments has peculiar interest. Sad

as may be the picture at home, when con-

trasted with the happy days that have past

or with what American institutions might

be, we know of no other country, all things

considered, that promises any greater

amount of general good to the masses of the

people than they may hope to find in our

own.


OLD ENGLAND, December 7, 1903.


The most striking contrasts of wealth and

poverty, knowledge and ignorance, refine-

ment and coarseness, virtue and vice, happi-

ness and misery, may be seen among the

people of Great Britain and Ireland, and

between the extremes,

"Wide as the poles asunder."

there is such variety of shades as would

puzzle the most accomplished word painter

to delineate. Equality of condition is a

figment of the imagination, which has never

yet been seen except in the dreams of utopian

theorists, and we may always expect to see

nature's law of variety exemplified in this

respect as in others but the most inveterate

optimist, who would take the trouble to

travel over this famous land and

see the condition of its people, would be

compelled to acknowledge that there is

grievous wrong somewhere, though it might

puzzle him to point it out and to prescribe

the remedy. There is most assuredly a

radical evil somewhere, which has thus far

baffled the skill of statesmen and philoso-

phers, and which fills thoughtful observers

with the most painful apprehensions. The

negro question is the bête noire of the United

States; the same may be said of millions of

the most degraded classes of these thickly

populated islands.


The wealth of the country is wonderful,

and it is increasing at an unprecedented

rate but it is in the possession chiefly of

the ancient aristocracy and the modern

manufacturers, traders and merchant princes

who have eclipsed the fame of all the

traders of the olden times. The palaces of

the nobility of the merchant princes in Lon-

don and the provinces abound in wealth, and

some of them are inestimable galleries of

art. Their occupants freely acknowledge

that the most wretched and debased occu-

pant of howell in the fever-dens of Lon-

don, Liverpool or Manchester, or of hut

in the country, is man and a brother; but,

alas, what vast difference there is in the

condition of the two classes of Englishmen.


One man in London owns mile square of

streets and houses, while thousands of others

have not a place to lay their heads. Anoth-

er in the country owns a farm of twenty-

three thousand acres, while thousands upon

thousands of laborers have to be crowded

together in cottages, which are so small as

to render decency and morality almost im-

possible.


In the Duke of Richmond's palace, we see

an extensive hall covered with yellow silk

and pictures in the richest and most costly

tapestry. The table services are of silver

and gold and the most elegant porcelain; the

ladies of the house spent six years in adorn-

ing grotto and the aviary is supplied with

every variety of rare and elegant birds. The

Duke of Devonshire's palace, at Chatsworth,

is well known to American tourists as one

of the most magnificent in England. Dr.


William W. Parker, of your city, who vis-

ited it in 1854, says: "Near the mansion is

'rockery,' as it is called, consisting of arti-

ficial cliffs, caves, deep and narrow passages,

&c. In going through one of these detours

ahead of my guide, I was suddenly arrested

by an immense rock covered with moss, and

commenced to climb over it; but judge my

surprise when the young man placed his

hand gently upon it, to find it rotate with

the most perfect ease, and thus permitting

us to pass. This assemblage of rocks cost

six hundred thousand dollars. Think of

that! I could but regret that this sum had

not been appropriated to the erection of a

noble college, with rich endowment, for the

poor youth of the land."


A better appropriation than this—as col-

leges are quite plentiful in Great Britain—

would be to the amelioration of the condi-

tion of the suffering poor, who need food

and raiment and comfortable homes, and

whose whole life is a constant struggle to

keep the wolf from their doors. The glass

conservatory at Chatsworth, which gave the

first idea of the Crystal Palace at Sydenham,

is 357 feet in length, 112 in breadth, and 81

He kindly informs us, that the constitutional amendment will be adopted by the North, and must be accepted by the people of the North as a condition of the acceptance of the South in admitting its representatives to Congress. The South understands the disposition of the Northern party very well; but does not see that their "requirements" are per consequence just.
